title: Streeter-Phelps dissolved-oxygen sag
summary: A biodegradable waste load decays downstream, pulling dissolved oxygen into a sag that recovers toward saturation.
question: After a waste load is discharged, how far does dissolved oxygen (DO) fall, and when/where does the minimum occur?
teaching: Two stocks track BOD and the oxygen deficit: BOD decay feeds the deficit while reaeration drains it, so the difference between the two rate constants sets the critical time. Look for a single deficit maximum and a matching oxygen minimum near day 2.3, followed by monotonic recovery toward saturation.

references.citation: Streeter, H. W., & Phelps, E. B. (1925). A study of the pollution and natural purification of the Ohio River. III. Factors concerned in the phenomena of oxidation and reaeration. Public Health Bulletin No. 146, U.S. Public Health Service.

title: Activated-sludge BOD removal with recycle
summary: A recycled activated-sludge basin grows biomass on incoming BOD and settles at a low effluent substrate concentration.
question: What effluent BOD and mixed-liquor solids does an activated-sludge basin achieve, and how does sludge recycle improve treatment?
teaching: Substrate and biomass are coupled by Monod growth: biomass consumes BOD, and the recycle fraction lengthens solids retention so the reactor keeps enough biomass to polish the effluent. Watch substrate fall from 250 mg/L to about 5 mg/L while MLSS rises toward 1000 mg/L; reducing recycle washes solids out.

references.citation: Monod, J. (1949). The growth of bacterial cultures. Annual Review of Microbiology, 3, 371–394.

title: Lake eutrophication: phosphorus, algae and dissolved oxygen
summary: External phosphorus feeds a self-limiting algal bloom whose growth, death and respiration drive a dissolved-oxygen sag.
question: How does an external phosphorus load drive an algal bloom that depletes dissolved oxygen, and how does phosphorus recycling on death close the loop?
teaching: Phosphorus, algae and dissolved oxygen form coupled loops: growth takes up P and produces oxygen, while respiration and decomposition consume it and death recycles P to the available pool. The bloom is capped by self-shading, so P first dips while algae climb, and DO sags as respiration overtakes photosynthesis plus reaeration.

references.citation: Vollenweider, R. A. (1975). Input-output models with special reference to the phosphorus loading concept in limnology. Schweizerische Zeitschrift für Hydrologie, 37(1), 53–84.

title: Groundwater contaminant transport with first-order decay
summary: A finite contaminant source charges an aquifer while advection and first-order decay drain it, then the plume declines after the source stops.
question: How does a contaminant mass evolve in an aquifer under advection and first-order decay, and how does the concentration respond when the source is removed?
teaching: One mass stock collects the injection and loses mass through discharge (residence time) and first-order decay. Loading stops at year 20, so the stock peaks there and then decays with both sinks acting; concentration is the same signal scaled by aquifer volume.

title: Logistic population growth with harvest
summary: Logistic growth and proportional harvest settle a population at the shaved carrying capacity, or collapse it when effort is high.
question: At what effort does a harvested population (fishery / invasive species) reach equilibrium, and when does it collapse?
teaching: The population grows logistically and loses individuals at a rate proportional to abundance. With r = 0.3 and effort = 0.15 the stable equilibrium is K(1 - effort/r) = 500, approached from below; raising effort to r removes the equilibrium and drives the stock to zero.

references.citation: Schaefer, M. B. (1954). Some aspects of the dynamics of populations important to the management of the commercial marine fisheries. Bulletin of the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission, 1(2), 27–56.

title: Reservoir sedimentation
summary: A reservoir traps sediment until its trap efficiency falls, and dredging shifts the fill toward a lower dynamic equilibrium.
question: How fast does a reservoir fill with sediment as trap efficiency declines, and how does maintenance dredging extend its life?
teaching: Sediment accumulates from the trapped fraction of the upstream load, while trap efficiency declines linearly as storage fills. Before dredging the reservoir follows an S-shaped fill toward capacity; dredging after year 25 removes sediment faster than the declining trap efficiency supplies it, so the stock peaks and settles at a new, lower level.

references.citation: Brune, G. M. (1953). Trap efficiency of reservoirs. Transactions, American Geophysical Union, 34(3), 407–418.

title: Watershed nonpoint-source nutrient export
summary: Seasonal precipitation drives runoff and land-use-dependent nutrient loads into a stream whose concentration follows the annual cycle.
question: How much nitrogen does a watershed deliver to a stream as a function of land use and seasonal precipitation, and what is the resulting in-stream concentration?
teaching: Runoff is the seasonal precipitation times a runoff coefficient, and each land use exports nutrients in proportion to its area and export coefficient, so urban land dominates the load. The stream mass is flushed at a one-month residence time, producing an annual oscillation in load and concentration with a peak each spring.

title: Atmospheric CO2 accumulation with carbon-climate feedback
summary: Constant emissions raise atmospheric CO2 until a concentration-dependent sink balances them, with warming weakening that sink.
question: Given constant emissions, to what new atmospheric CO2 and temperature does the Earth system settle once a carbon-climate feedback weakens natural uptake?
teaching: CO2 is a single stock fed by emissions and drained by natural uptake proportional to the excess over preindustrial concentration. A carbon-climate feedback reduces uptake as temperature rises, so the equilibrium sits higher than it would without warming; the CO2 trajectory is monotonic and flattens toward roughly 412 ppm by 2200.
